nodes.name: Split Cartan modular curve $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$
nodes.statement: For a prime integer $p$, let $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ be the modular curve defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ attached to the congruence subgroup of level $p$ $$ \Gamma_{\operatorname{split}}(p)=\left\{ \left (\begin{array}{cc}a &b\\c& d\end{array}\right)\in\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\colon b\equiv c\equiv 0 \text{ or }a\equiv d\equiv 0\right\}\,. $$
differentia: attached to the congruence subgroup of level $p$
nodes.statement_short: $X_{split}(p)$ is the modular curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ attached to the split Cartan congruence subgroup $\Gamma_{split}(p)$ of level $p$.

nodes.name: $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)\simeq X_0^+(p^2)$
nodes.statement: It is well-known that $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is isomorphic over $\mathbb{Q}$ to the modular curve $X_0^+(p^2):=X_0(p^2)/w_{p^2}$, where $w_{p^2}$ stands for the Fricke involution.
conclusions: $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is isomorphic over $\mathbb{Q}$ to the modular curve $X_0^+(p^2):=X_0(p^2)/w_{p^2}$
nodes.statement_short: The split Cartan curve of level $p$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-isomorphic to $X_0^+(p^2)$, the quotient of $X_0(p^2)$ by the Fricke involution.

nodes.name: Genus of $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$
nodes.statement: The genus of this curve is positive when $p\geq 11$ and, in this case, it is at least $2$.
conclusions: The genus of this curve is positive
it is at least $2$

nodes.name: Automorphism group of split Cartan modular curves
nodes.statement: Assume that the genus of $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is positive. Then, $$\operatorname{Aut}(X_{\operatorname{split}}(p))=\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X_{\operatorname{split}}(p))\simeq\left\{\begin{array}{cc} \{1\} & \text{if $p>11$,}\\[5 pt] (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2 & \text{if $p=11$.}\end{array}\right. $$
assumptions: Assume that the genus of $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is positive.
conclusions: $$\operatorname{Aut}(X_{\operatorname{split}}(p))=\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X_{\operatorname{split}}(p))\simeq\left\{\begin{array}{cc} \{1\} & \text{if $p>11$,}\\[5 pt] (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2 & \text{if $p=11$.}\end{array}\right. $$
nodes.statement_short: For positive genus, every automorphism of $X_{split}(p)$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$; the group is trivial for $p>11$ and $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$ for $p=11$.
nodes.label: teo

nodes.name: Twist of a newform by a Dirichlet character (Atkin-Li)
nodes.statement: We recall that, for a normalized newform $f=\sum_{n\geq 1} a_n q^n\in S_2(\Gamma_1(N))^{\operatorname{new}}$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$ of conductor $N'$, the function $$f_\chi:=\sum_{n\geq 1} \chi(n)a_n q^n$$ is a cusp form in $S_2(\Gamma_1(\operatorname{lcm} (N, {N'}^2))$ (cf. Proposition 3.1 de \cite{Atkin}).
assumptions: a normalized  newform $f=\sum_{n\geq 1} a_n q^n\in S_2(\Gamma_1(N))^{\operatorname{new}}$
conclusions: the function $$f_\chi:=\sum_{n\geq 1} \chi(n)a_n q^n$$ is a cusp form in $S_2(\Gamma_1(\operatorname{lcm} (N, {N'}^2))$
nodes.statement_short: The twist $f_\chi$ of a weight-2 newform of level $N$ by a character of conductor $N'$ is a cusp form of level $\mathrm{lcm}(N,N'^2)$.

nodes.name: $q=e^{2\pi i z}$
nodes.statement: Here, as usual, $q=e^{2\pi \,i\,z}$.

nodes.name: Twisted newform $f\otimes\chi$
nodes.statement: Let $f\otimes \chi$ denote the unique normalized newform with $q$-expansion $\sum_{n\geq 1} b_n q^n$ that satisfies $b_{\ell}=\chi(\ell) a_{\ell}$ for all primes $\ell\nmid N\cdot N'$.
differentia: $b_{\ell}=\chi(\ell) a_{\ell}$ for all primes  $\ell\nmid N\cdot N'$

nodes.name: Level of $f\otimes\chi$ divides level of $f_\chi$
nodes.statement: If $f\otimes \chi$ is a newform of level $M$ and $f_\chi$ has level $M'$, then $M|M'$. Moreover, if $M=M'$, then $f_\chi=f\otimes\chi$.
conclusions: if $M=M'$, then $f_\chi=f\otimes\chi$

nodes.name: $\operatorname{New}_N$
nodes.statement: Let $\operatorname{New}_N$ denote the set of normalized newforms in $S_2(\Gamma_0(N))^{\operatorname{new}}$.

nodes.name: Fricke eigenvalue $\varepsilon(f)$ and $\operatorname{New}_N^+$
nodes.statement: For $f\in\operatorname{New}_N$, $\varepsilon(f)$ denotes the eigenvalue of $f$ under the action of the Fricke involution $w_N$ and set $\operatorname{New}_N^+=\{f\in \operatorname{New}_N\colon \varepsilon(f)=1\}$.

nodes.name: $S_2(f)$
nodes.statement: For a cusp form $f=\sum_n b_n q^n \in S_2(\Gamma_0(N))$ such that $\mathbb{Q}(\{b_n\})$ is a number field, $S_2(f)$ denotes the $\mathbb{C}$-vector space of cusp forms spanned by $f$ and its Galois conjugates.
differentia: spanned  by  $f$ and its  Galois conjugates

nodes.name: Shimura abelian variety $A_f$
nodes.statement: In the particular case that $f\in\operatorname{New}_N$, $A_f$ stands for the abelian variety attached to $f$ by Shimura.

nodes.name: $A_f$ is a quotient of $J_0(N)$
nodes.statement: It is well-known that $A_f$ is a quotient of $J_0(N):=\operatorname{Jac} (X_0(N))$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ and the pull-back of $\Omega^1_{A_f/\mathbb{Q}}$ is the $\mathbb{Q}$-vector subspace of elements in $S_2(f) dq/q$ with rational $q$-expansion, i.e. $S_2(f) dq/q\cap\mathbb{Q}[[q]]$.
conclusions: $A_f$ is a quotient of $J_0(N):=\operatorname{Jac} (X_0(N))$  defined over  $\mathbb{Q}$
the  pull-back of $\Omega^1_{A_f/\mathbb{Q}}$  is the $\mathbb{Q}$-vector subspace of elements in  $S_2(f) dq/q$ with rational $q$-expansion
nodes.statement_short: $A_f$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-quotient of $J_0(N)$, and its regular differentials pull back to the rational elements of $S_2(f)dq/q$.

nodes.name: $\operatorname{End}_\mathbb{Q}(A_f)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ is totally real
nodes.statement: Moreover, the endomorphism algebra $\operatorname{End}_\mathbb{Q}(A_f)\otimes \mathbb{Q}$ is a totally real number field.
conclusions: the endomorphism algebra $\operatorname{End}_\mathbb{Q}(A_f)\otimes \mathbb{Q}$ is a totally real number field

nodes.name: Quadratic character $\chi$ of conductor $p$ and field $K$
nodes.statement: \vskip0.2 cm From now on, we assume $p\geq 11$ and $\chi$ denotes the quadratic Dirichlet character of conductor $p$, i.e. the Dirichlet character attached to the quadratic number field $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p^*})$, where $p^*=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}$.
nodes.genus: the  quadratic Dirichlet character of conductor $p$
nodes.statement_short: Standing assumption $p\ge 11$; $\chi$ is the quadratic character of conductor $p$, attached to $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p^*})$.

nodes.name: Twisting by $\chi$ permutes newforms of level $p^2$ and $p$
nodes.statement: The map $f\mapsto f\otimes \chi$ is a permutation of the set $\operatorname{New}_{p^2}\cup\operatorname{New}_p$. Under this bijection, there is a unique newform $f$, up to Galois conjugation, such that $f=f\otimes \chi$ when $p\equiv 3 \pmod 4$.
conclusions: The map $f\mapsto f\otimes \chi$ is a permutation of the set $\operatorname{New}_{p^2}\cup\operatorname{New}_p$
there is a unique newform $f$, up to Galois conjugation, such that $f=f\otimes \chi$
nodes.statement_short: Twisting by $\chi$ permutes $\mathrm{New}_{p^2}\cup\mathrm{New}_p$; for $p\equiv 3$ mod 4 there is exactly one fixed newform up to conjugation (the CM one).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Since $f_\chi\in S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))$ for $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}\cup\operatorname{New}_p$ (cf. Theorem 3.1 of \cite{Atkin}), the level of $f\otimes\chi$ divides $p^2$ and, thus, the map is well defined. The injectivity follows from the fact that $(f\otimes\chi)\otimes\chi=f$. The condition $f=f\otimes\chi$ amounts to saying that $f$ has complex multiplication (CM) by the imaginary quadratic field $K$ attached to $\chi$, i.e. $p\equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and, moreover, $f$ is obtained from a Hecke character $\psi$ whose conductor is the ideal of $K$ of norm $p$, which implies $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}$. Since $f$ has trivial Nebentypus, the Hecke character $\psi$ is unique up to Galois conjugation.
nodes.statement_short: Atkin-Li gives level dividing $p^2$; injectivity since twisting twice is the identity; fixed points are CM forms from a unique Hecke character of conductor of norm $p$.

nodes.name: Well-definedness via Atkin-Li: the twist has level dividing
nodes.statement: Since $f_\chi\in S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))$ for $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}\cup\operatorname{New}_p$ (cf. Theorem 3.1 of \cite{Atkin}), the level of $f\otimes\chi$ divides $p^2$ and, thus, the map is well defined.
nodes.statement_short: Well-definedness via Atkin-Li: the twist has level dividing $p^2$

nodes.name: Injectivity since twisting twice by $\chi$ is the identity
nodes.statement: The injectivity follows from the fact that $(f\otimes\chi)\otimes\chi=f$.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity since twisting twice by $\chi$ is the identity

nodes.name: Fixed points are CM forms from a Hecke character, unique up
nodes.statement: The condition $f=f\otimes\chi$ amounts to saying that $f$ has complex multiplication (CM) by the imaginary quadratic field $K$ attached to $\chi$, i.e. $p\equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and, moreover, $f$ is obtained from a Hecke character $\psi$ whose conductor is the ideal of $K$ of norm $p$, which implies $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}$. Since $f$ has trivial Nebentypus, the Hecke character $\psi$ is unique up to Galois conjugation.
nodes.statement_short: Fixed points are CM forms from a Hecke character, unique up to conjugation

nodes.name: Twisting does not preserve Fricke eigenvalue
nodes.statement: The above map does not preserve the eigenvalue of the corresponding Fricke involution, i.e. it may be that $\varepsilon(f)$ and $\varepsilon(f\otimes \chi)$ are different.

nodes.name: Inner twists of non-CM newforms of level $p^2$, $p$
nodes.statement: Let $f \in \operatorname{New}_{p^2}\cup \operatorname{New}_p$ without CM. If $f$ has an inner twist $\chi'\neq 1$, i.e. $f\otimes \chi'={}^{\sigma} f$ for some $\sigma\in G_\mathbb{Q}:=\mathrm{Gal} (\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$, then $\chi'=\chi$ because $\chi'$ must be a quadratic character of conductor dividing $p^2$. In such a case, $\operatorname{End} (A_f)\otimes\mathbb{Q}=\operatorname{End}_K(A_f)\otimes \mathbb{Q}$ is a non commutative algebra. Otherwise, $\operatorname{End} (A_f)\otimes\mathbb{Q}=\operatorname{End}_\mathbb{Q}(A_f)\otimes \mathbb{Q}$ is a totally real umber field.
nodes.statement_short: A non-CM $f$ can only have $\chi$ as inner twist; then $\mathrm{End}(A_f)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ is noncommutative and defined over $K$, otherwise a totally real field.

nodes.name: CM newform of level $p^2$
nodes.statement: If $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}$ has CM, then the dimension of $A_f$ is the class number of $K$, $A_f$ has all its endomorphisms defined over the Hilbert class field of $K$ and $\operatorname{End}_K(A_f)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ is the CM field $\operatorname{End}_\mathbb{Q}(A_f)\otimes K$ which only contains the roots of the unity $\pm 1$ (cf. Theorem 1.2 of of \cite{gola011} and part (3) in Proposition 3.2 of \cite{Yang2}). Moreover, $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+$ if, and only if, $p\equiv 3\pmod 8$ (cf. Corollary 6.3 of \cite{Yang1}).
nodes.origin_citation: Gonzalez-Lario Thm 1.2; Yang Prop 3.2(3); Yang Cor 6.3
nodes.statement_short: For the CM newform, $\dim A_f=h_K$, endomorphisms are defined over the Hilbert class field, the CM field has only $\pm1$ as roots of unity, and $f\in\mathrm{New}^+$ iff $p\equiv 3$ mod 8.

nodes.name: Isogenies between $A_{f_1}$ and $A_{f_2}$
nodes.statement: For two distinct $f_1, f_2\in(\operatorname{New}_{p^2}\cup\operatorname{New}_p)/G_\mathbb{Q}$, the abelian varieties $A_{f_1}$ and $A_{f_2}$ are nonisogenous over $\mathbb{Q}$ and are isogenous if, and only if, $f_1\otimes \chi={}^{\sigma} f_2$ for some $\sigma\in G_\mathbb{Q}$ (see Proposition 4.2 of \cite{goji}) and, in this particular case, there is an isogeny defined over $K$.
nodes.statement_short: Distinct $A_{f_1},A_{f_2}$ are never $\mathbb{Q}$-isogenous, and are isogenous (over $K$) iff $f_2$ is a conjugate of $f_1\otimes\chi$.

nodes.name: Decomposition of $J_0^+(p^2)$
nodes.statement: The abelian variety $J_0^+(p^2):=\operatorname{Jac} (X_0^+(p^2))$ splits over $\mathbb{Q}$ as the product $(J_0(p^2)^{\operatorname{new}})^{\langle w_{p^2}\rangle}\times J_0(p)$. More precisely, \begin{equation} J_0^+(p^2)\stackrel{\mathbb{Q}}\sim \prod_{f\in(\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup\operatorname{New}_p)/G_{\mathbb{Q}}} A_f\,. \end{equation}
conclusions: $J_0^+(p^2):=\operatorname{Jac} (X_0^+(p^2))$ splits over $\mathbb{Q}$ as the product $(J_0(p^2)^{\operatorname{new}})^{\langle w_{p^2}\rangle}\times J_0(p)$
nodes.statement_short: $J_0^+(p^2)$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-isogenous to the product of $A_f$ over $f\in(\mathrm{New}^+_{p^2}\cup\mathrm{New}_p)/G_\mathbb{Q}$.

nodes.name: Splitting of $J_0^+(p^2)$
nodes.statement: J_0^+(p^2)\stackrel{\mathbb{Q}}\sim \prod_{f\in(\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup\operatorname{New}_p)/G_{\mathbb{Q}}} A_f\,.
nodes.label: split

nodes.name: Fricke eigenforms from oldforms of level $p$
nodes.statement: Each $f\in \operatorname{New}_p$ provides a vector subspace of $S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))^{\operatorname{old}}$ of dimension $2$ genera\-ted by $f(q)$ and $f(q^p)$. The normalized cusp forms $f(q)+p\,\varepsilon(f) f(q^p)$ and $f(q)-p\,\varepsilon(f) f(q^p)$ are eigenforms for all Hecke operators $T_m$ with $p\nmid m$ and the Fricke involution $w_{p^2}$ with eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$ respectively.
conclusions: The normalized cusp forms $f(q)+p\,\varepsilon(f) f(q^p)$ and $f(q)-p\,\varepsilon(f) f(q^p)$ are eigenforms  for all Hecke operators $T_m$ with $p\nmid m$ and the Fricke involution $w_{p^2}$ with eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$ respectively
nodes.statement_short: Each level-$p$ newform gives a 2-dim oldspace at level $p^2$ split into $w_{p^2}$-eigenforms $f(q)\pm p\varepsilon(f)f(q^p)$.

nodes.name: Decomposition of regular differentials of $J_0^+(p^2)$
nodes.statement: The splitting of $J_0^+(p^2)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ provides the following decomposition for its vector space of regular differentials \begin{equation} \Omega^1_{J_0^+(p^2)}=\left(\bigoplus_{f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+/G_\mathbb{Q}}S_2(f(q))\frac{dq}{q}\right)\bigoplus\left(\bigoplus_{f\in\operatorname{New}_{p}/G_\mathbb{Q}} S_2(f(q)+p\,\varepsilon(f)f(q^p))\frac{dq}{q}\right)\,. \end{equation}
conclusions: the following decomposition for its vector space of regular differentials
nodes.statement_short: Regular differentials of $J_0^+(p^2)$ decompose into the spaces $S_2(f)dq/q$ for $f\in\mathrm{New}^+_{p^2}$ and $S_2(f(q)+p\varepsilon(f)f(q^p))dq/q$ for $f\in\mathrm{New}_p$.

nodes.name: Decomposition of $\Omega^1_{J_0^+(p^2)}$
nodes.statement: \Omega^1_{J_0^+(p^2)}=\left(\bigoplus_{f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+/G_\mathbb{Q}}S_2(f(q))\frac{dq}{q}\right)\bigoplus\left(\bigoplus_{f\in\operatorname{New}_{p}/G_\mathbb{Q}} S_2(f(q)+p\,\varepsilon(f)f(q^p))\frac{dq}{q}\right)\,.
nodes.label: diferencial

nodes.name: Genera $g^+$ and $g_0$
nodes.statement: Let $g^+$ and $g_0$ be the genus of the curves $ X_0^+(p^2)$ and $X_0(p)$, respectively.

nodes.name: Genus formulas for $X_0^+(p^2)$ and $X_0(p)$
nodes.statement: From the genus formula for these curves, one obtains the following values $$ \begin{array}{c|c|c|} p & g^+ &g_0\\ \hline\hline p\equiv 1 \pmod{12} &\displaystyle{\frac{(p-1)(p-7)}{24}} & \displaystyle{\frac{p-13}{12}}\\[6 pt] p\equiv 5 \pmod{12} &\displaystyle{ \frac{(p-3)(p-5)}{24} } & \displaystyle{\frac{p-5}{12} }\\[6 pt] p\equiv 7 \pmod{12} & \displaystyle{ \frac{(p-1)(p-7)}{24} }&\displaystyle{\frac{p-7}{12}} \\[6 pt] p\equiv 11 \pmod{12} &\displaystyle{ \frac{(p-3)(p-5)}{24} } & \displaystyle{\frac{p+1}{12}}\\\hline \end{array} $$
assumptions: From the genus formula for these curves
conclusions: one obtains the following values
nodes.statement_short: Table of $g^+$ and $g_0$ as functions of $p$ modulo 12.

nodes.name: Hyperelliptic split Cartan curves
nodes.statement: Assume $p\geq 11 $. Then, $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is hyperelliptic if, and only if, $p=11$. Moreover, one has $$\operatorname{Aut} (X_{\operatorname{split}}(11))=\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X_{\operatorname{split}}(11))\simeq (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2\,. $$
conclusions: $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is hyperelliptic if, and only if,  $p=11$
$$\operatorname{Aut} (X_{\operatorname{split}}(11))=\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X_{\operatorname{split}}(11))\simeq (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2\,. $$
nodes.statement_short: For $p\ge 11$, $X_{split}(p)$ is hyperelliptic only for $p=11$, where its automorphism group is $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$, all defined over $\mathbb{Q}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: Assume $X_0^+(p^2)$ is hyperelliptic. By applying Lemma 3.25 of \cite{BGGP}, we obtain $g^+\leq 10$, which implies $p\leq 19$. We have $g^+=2$ if, and only if, $p=11$ and, thus, the curve $X_0^+(11^2)$ is hyperelliptic. For $p>11$, on has $g^+>2$ and, moreover, $p>13$ because $X_0^+(13^2)$ is a plane quartic (cf. \cite{Baran}). Lemma 2.5 of \cite{BGGP} states that there is a basis $f_1,\cdots, f_{g^+}$ of $S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))^{\langle w_{p^2}\rangle}$ with rational $q$-expansions satisfying \begin{equation} f_i(q)=\left\{\begin{array}{cr} q^i+ O(q^i)&\text{ if the cusp $\infty$ is not a Weierstrass point of $X_0^+ (p^2)$,}\\q^{2 i-1}+ O(q^{2i-1})& \text{otherwise.}\end{array} \right. \end{equation} Moreover, for any such a basis, the functions on $X_0 ^+(p^2)$ defined by $$ x=\frac{f_{g^+}}{f_{g^+-1}}\,,\quad y=\frac{ q dx/dq}{f_{g^+-1}}\,, $$ satisfy $y^2=P(x)$ for a unique squarefree polynomial $P(X)\in\mathbb{Q}[X]$ which has degree $2g^++1$ or $2g^++2$ depending on whether $\infty$ is a Weierstrass point or not. The first part of the statement follows from the fact that, for $p=17$ and $p=19$, the vector space $S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))^{\langle w_{p^2}\rangle}$ does not have any bases as in (\ref{congq}). Now, we consider $p=11$. In this case, $|\operatorname{New}_{11^2}|=|\operatorname{New}_{11}|=1$. Let $f_1\in\operatorname{New}_{11^2}^+$ and let $f_2\in\operatorname{New}_{11}$. The newform $f_1$ is the one attached to the elliptic curve $E_1/\mathbb{Q}$ of conductor $11^2$ with CM by $\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-11})/2]$, and $f_2$ is the newform attached to an elliptic curve $E_2/\mathbb{Q}$ of conductor $11$ without CM. Since $\varepsilon(f_2)=-1$, the cusp forms $f_1(q)$ and $h(q)=f_2(q)-11 f_2(q^{11})$ are a basis of $S_2(\Gamma_0(11^2))^{\langle w_{11^2}\rangle}$. Take the following functions on $X_0^+(11^2)$ $$ x=\frac{h}{f_1}=1 - 2 q + 2 q^3 - 2 q^5 + O(q^5)\,,\quad y=-2 \frac{q\,dx/q}{f_1}=4 - 8 q^2 + 8 q^3 + 24 q^4 - 32 q^5+ O(q^5)\,. $$ Using $q$-expansions, we get the following equation for $X_0^+(11^2)$: \begin{equation} y^2= x^6 -7 x^4+11 x^2+11\,. \end{equation}The maps $(x,y)\mapsto (\pm x,\pm y) $ provide a subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}_\mathbb{Q}(X_0^+(11^2))$ isomorphic to $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2$. Since $\operatorname{Aut}_{\overline\mathbb{Q}}(X_0^+(11^2))$ is a finite subgroup of $\operatorname{End}(E_1)\times \operatorname{End}(E_2)\simeq \mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-11})/2]\times\mathbb{Z}$, we have that it must be a subgroup of $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2$, which proves the second part of the statement.
nodes.statement_short: Genus bound from BGGP reduces to $p\le 19$; the BGGP basis criterion rules out $p=17,19$. For $p=11$ an explicit genus-2 model $y^2=x^6-7x^4+11x^2+11$ and the endomorphism rings of $E_1,E_2$ give $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.5 of BGGP (hyperelliptic equations from $q$-expansions)

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: The modular curve $X_0(p^2)$ has $p+1$ cusps. Only the cusps $\infty$ and $0$ are defined over $\mathbb{Q}$. The remaining cusps $1/p,\cdots, (p-1)/p$ are defined over the $p$-th cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$. The Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)/\mathbb{Q})$ acts transitively on this set, and the cusp $w_{p^2}(i/p)=(p-i)/p$ is the complex conjugate of the cusp $i/p$ (cf. \cite{Ogg}). Hence, among the $(p+1)/2$ cusps of $X_0^+(p^2)$ the cusp $\infty$ is the only one defined over the quadratic field $K$. Let $u$ be an automorphism of $X_0^+(p^2)$ such that $u(\infty)$ is a cusp. By Lemma \ref{defi}, $u(\infty)$ is defined over $K$ and, thus, $u(\infty)=\infty$. Let $\mathbb{Q} [[q]]$ be the completion of the local ring ${\mathcal O}_{X_0^+(p^2),\infty}$ with respect to the local parameter $q$. If $u(\infty)$ is the cusp $\infty$, then $u^*(q)=\zeta_m q+\sum_{n>1} c_i q^i$, where $\zeta_m$ is a primitive $m$-th root of unity and, thus, $u$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q} (\zeta_m)$. Since the unique roots of unity in $K$ are $\pm 1$, it follows that $u$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$. Now, we will prove that, if $u\in\operatorname{Aut}_\mathbb{Q}(X_0^+(p^2))$ is nontrivial, then $u(\infty)\neq \infty$. For the hyperelliptic case $p=11$, the cusp $\infty$ has $(1,4)$ as $(x,y)$ coordinates in the equation given in (\ref{eq}). Hence, $\infty$ is not a fixed point for any of the three nontrivial involutions of $X_{0}^+(11^2)$. Let $p>11$. Since $X_0^+(p^2)$ is nonhyperelliptic and, by Lemma \ref{overQ}, $u$ is an involution, we can exclude the case where all eigenvalues of $u$ acting on $\Omega^1_{J_0^+(p^2)}$ are equal to $-1$ and, thus, $u$ must have eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$ acting on this vector space. The vector space of cusp forms $\Omega^1_{J_0^+(p^2)} {q}/{dq}$ has a basis of normalized eigenforms (see (\ref{diferencial})). Since $u$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$, $u$ commutes with the Hecke operators and, thus, there are two normalized eigenforms such that their corresponding regular differentials $\omega_1=(1+\sum_{n>1} a_n q^n)dq$ and $\omega_2=(1+\sum_{n>1} b_n q^n)dq$ satisfy $u^*(\omega_1)=\omega_1$ and $u^*(\omega_2)=-\omega_2$. Hence, $u$ sends $\omega_1+\omega_2$, which does vanish at $\infty$, to $\omega_1-\omega_2$, which vanishes at $\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: $\infty$ is the only cusp over $K$, so $u(\infty)=\infty$ and $u$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$. Then a $\pm1$-eigendifferential argument (or the explicit model for $p=11$) shows $u$ cannot fix $\infty$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8
nodes.statement: Assume that there is a nontrivial automorphism $u$ of $X_0^+(p^2)$ whose order $m$ is odd. Let $X_u$ be the quotient curve $X_0^+(p^2)/ u$ and denote by $ g_u$ its genus. Next, we find a positive lower bound $t$ for $g_u$. The endomorphism algebra $\operatorname{End}_K(J_0^+(p^2))\otimes \mathbb{Q}$ is the product of some noncommutative algebras and some number fields $E_f=\operatorname{End}_K (A_f)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ attached to the newforms $f$ lying in a certain subset ${\mathcal S}$ of $ (\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup \operatorname{New}_p)/G_\mathbb{Q}$. The set ${\mathcal S}$ is formed by newforms $f$ without CM such that $f\otimes \chi\notin \operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup\operatorname{New}_p$ ($E_f=\operatorname{End}_\mathbb{Q}(A_f)$ is a totally real number field) and by a newform $f$ with CM by $K$ if $p\equiv 3\pmod 8$ ($E_f=\operatorname{End}_\mathbb{Q}(A_f)\otimes K$ is a CM field). For $f\in{\mathcal S}$, the unique root of unities contained in $E_f$ are $\pm 1$. Since $m$ is odd, the automorphism $u$ must act on each $E_f$ as the identity and, thus, we have $$t:= \sum_{f\in {\mathcal S}}\dim A_f\leq g_u\,.$$ An easy computation provides the following values for $t$: $$ \begin{array}{c|ccccc|} p& 17 &19 &23 & 29& 31\\\hline\hline g^+&7 & 9& 15& 26 & 30\\ t&5 & 5& 7& 15 & 12\\ \hline \end{array} $$ Applying Riemann-Hurwitz formula, $$\displaystyle{m\leq \frac{g^+-1}{g_u-1}\leq \frac{g^+-1}{t-1}}<3\,,$$which yields a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: an odd-order $u$ acts trivially on the factors with only $\pm1$ roots of unity, giving $g_u\ge t$; Riemann-Hurwitz then forces $m<3$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Assume that, for $p\in\{17,19,23,29,31\}$, there is a nontrivial automorphism $u\in\operatorname{Aut}_K(X_0^+(p^2))$. By Lemma \ref{invo}, we can suppose that $u$ is an involution. Let $g_u$ be the genus of the quotient curve $X_0^+(p^2)/u$. We know that $u$ has at most $12$ fixed points. By Riemann-Hurwitz formula, we get that the number of fixed points by $u$ must be even, say $2r$, and, moreover, $$ g_u=\frac{g^++1-r}{2}\,,\quad 0\leq r\leq 6\,. $$ If $g^+$ is even, then $u$ can have $2$, $6$ or $10$ ramification points, while for the case $g^+$ odd, $u$ can have $0$, $4$, $8$ or $12$ such points. For a prime $\ell\neq p$, the curve $X=X_0^+(p^2)$ has good reduction at $\ell$. Let $\widetilde{X}$ be the reduction of $X$ modulo $\ell$. We write $$ N_{\ell}(n):=1+\ell^n-\sum_{i=1}^{2 g^+}\alpha_i^n\,, $$ where $\alpha_1,\cdots,\alpha_{2 g^+}$ are the roots of polynomial $$ \prod_{f\in \operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup\operatorname{New}_p}(x^2-a_{\ell}(f) x+\ell) $$ and $a_{\ell}(f)$ is the $\ell$-th Fourier coefficient of $f$. By Eichler-Shimura congruence, $N_{\ell}(n)=|\widetilde{X}(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^n})|$. Let $\mathfrak l$ be a prime of $K$ over $\ell$ with residue degree $s$. The reduction of $X\otimes K$ modulo $\mathfrak l$ is $\widetilde X\otimes \mathbb{F}_{\ell^s}$ which has an involution, say $\widetilde u$, with at most $2r$ fixed points. The automorphism $\widetilde u$ acts on the set $\widetilde{X}(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^{s\, n}})$ as a permutation. If $Q\in \cup_{i=1}^n\widetilde X(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^{ s\,i}})$, then the set ${\mathcal S}_Q=\{ \widetilde{u}^i(Q)\colon 1\leq i \leq 2\}$ is contained in $ \cup_{i=1}^n\widetilde X(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^{ s\,i}})$ and its cardinality is equal to $1$ or $2$ according to $Q$ is a fixed point of $\widetilde u$ or not. Hence, almost all integers $R_{\ell}(n):=|\cup_{i=1}^n\widetilde X(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^{ s\,i}})|$, $n\geq 1$, are equivalent to the number of fixed points of $\widetilde{u}$ mod $2$ and, moreover, the sequence $\{R_\ell (n)\}_{n\geq 1}$ can only contain at most $2r$ or $2r-1$ changes of parity depending on whether $N_{\ell}(s)$ is even or odd. In other words, the sequence of integers $\{ P_\ell(n)\}_{n\geq 1}$ defined by $$0\leq P_\ell (n)\leq 1\,\,\text{ and }\,\, P_{\ell}(n)=R_{\ell}(n+1)-R_{\ell}(n)\pmod 2\,,$$ can only contain at most $2r$ or $2r-1$ ones according to $N_{\ell^s}$ being even or odd. Note that the integer $R_{\ell}(n+1)-R_{\ell}(n)$ can be obtained from the sequence $\{ N_\ell (s\, n)\}$ by using $$\widetilde X (\mathbb{F}_{\ell ^{s\,d_1}})\cap \widetilde X(\mathbb{F}_{\ell ^{s\, d_2}})=\widetilde X (\mathbb{F}_{\ell ^{s\,\gcd(d_1,d_2)}})\,,\quad\text{ and if } d_1|d_2 \text{ then }\widetilde X (\mathbb{F}_{\ell ^{s\,d_1}})\cup \widetilde X (\mathbb{F}_{\ell ^{s\,d_2}})=\widetilde X(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^{s\,d_2}})\,. $$ More precisely, if $\{p_1,\cdots,p_r\}$ is the set of primes dividing $n+1$ and we put $d_i=(n+1)/p_i$ for $1\leq i\leq r$, then $$ R_{\ell}(n+1)-R_{\ell}(n)= P_\ell (s(n+1))-\sum_ {j=1}^r (-1)^{r-1} \sum_{1\leq i_1<\cdots<i_j\leq r} P_\ell (s \gcd(d_{i_1},\cdots,d_{i_j}))\,.$$ For the five possibilities for $p$, we have: \vskip 0.2 cm { $p=31$:} $g^+=30$, $2r\leq 10$ and $\ell=2$ splits in $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-31})$. One has $$ N_2(1)=9\,,\qquad \sum_{n\leq 36}P_2(n)=10\,. $$ \vskip 0.2 cm {$p=29$:} $g^+=26$, $2r\leq 10$ and $\ell=2$ is inert in $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{29})$. One has $$ N_2(2)=42\,,\qquad \sum_{n\leq 42}P_2(n)=11\,. $$ \vskip 0.2 cm { $p=23$:} $g^+=15$, $2r\leq 12$ and $\ell=2$ splits in $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-23})$. One has $$ N_2(1)=8\,,\qquad \sum_{n\leq 38}P_2(n)=13\,. $$ \vskip 0.2 cm { $p=19$:} $g^+=9$, $2r\leq 12$ and $\ell=2$ is inert in $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-19})$. One has $$N_2(2)=22\,,\qquad \sum_{n\leq 46 } P_2(n)=13\,. $$ \vskip 0.2 cm { $p=17$:} $g^+=7$, $2r\leq 12$ and $\ell=2$ splits in $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{17})$. One has $$ N_2(1)=6\,,\quad\quad\sum_{n\leq 46}P_2(n)=13\,. $$ So, we can discard the five cases considered and the statement is proved.

nodes.statement: \vskip 0.2 cm { $p=31$:} $g^+=30$, $2r\leq 10$ and $\ell=2$ splits in $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-31})$. One has $$ N_2(1)=9\,,\qquad \sum_{n\leq 36}P_2(n)=10\,. $$
nodes.statement_short: $p=31$: 10 parity changes exceed bound

nodes.name: $p=29$: 11 parity changes
nodes.statement: \vskip 0.2 cm {$p=29$:} $g^+=26$, $2r\leq 10$ and $\ell=2$ is inert in $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{29})$. One has $$ N_2(2)=42\,,\qquad \sum_{n\leq 42}P_2(n)=11\,. $$
nodes.statement_short: $p=29$: 11 parity changes
